prompt: A team holds 50 requests a second for ten minutes and compares the 95th percentile with the 200 ms in its requirement. Which test is that?

choices.text: A stress test
choices.why: A stress test keeps climbing past the expected load; this one holds it.

choices.text: A soak test, since it lasts ten minutes
choices.why: A soak holds the load for hours, and asks what drifts rather than whether a threshold holds.

choices.text: A load test
choices.why: Right. The expected load, held, judged against thresholds written down first.

choices.text: A spike test at a fixed rate
choices.why: A spike is a sudden jump and back; a constant rate has no jump in it.

prompt: Past 300 requests a second, a stress test sees the server answer the excess at once with 503 and recover as soon as the load drops. How should the result be read?
hint: A stress test is read for where and how.

choices.text: It failed well, with a breaking point near 300 a second
choices.why: Right. A quick refusal and a recovery on its own are the good manner; 300 is the capacity it found.

choices.text: It failed, because there were errors during the run
choices.why: Errors are expected past the breaking point. What would fail it is a bad manner: corruption, or no recovery.

choices.text: It passed, so the server has no limit
choices.why: It found the limit: 300 a second. Every system has one.

choices.text: It needs a soak test first
choices.why: A soak asks a different question, about drift over hours, and does not change how this one is read.

prompt: Match each test to the question it answers.
hint: The table at the end of "Five tests, five questions".

pairs.right: does it meet the requirement at the expected load?
where and how does it break?
does it survive a sudden crowd and recover?

right_distractors: does it do what the specification says?

prompt: At the expected load, a soak test reads a 95th percentile of 80 ms in its first hour and 190 ms in its eighth. The threshold is 200 ms. What do you report?
hint: A soak test is read as a trend.

choices.text: A pass, because each hour stayed under 200 ms
choices.why: Each hour did, and the trend says the ninth or tenth will not. A soak test exists to see exactly this.

choices.text: A finding: something accumulates
choices.why: Right. The last hour does not look like the first, so something grows with time, and it will cross the threshold.

choices.text: A stress result, since the times went up
choices.why: The load never rose; the time did. Rising times at a flat load are what a soak looks for.

choices.text: Nothing yet, because no request failed
choices.why: A soak is judged on drift, and 80 ms becoming 190 ms is drift.

prompt: What does a spike test check that a look at the peak alone misses?
hint: The load is normal again. Are the times?

choices.text: Whether the peak was high enough to be a spike
choices.why: The height is chosen in advance, from the expected crowd. It is the input, not the finding.

choices.text: The highest throughput the system sustains
choices.why: That is a capacity, found by a stress staircase.

choices.text: Whether memory grows over the night
choices.why: Drift over hours is a soak test.

choices.text: How soon the times are normal after it
choices.why: Right. A queue left by the spike delays the people who arrive at an ordinary moment afterwards.

prompt: Why does hammer.py start each request in a thread of its own, instead of sending the next one when the last answer arrives?
hint: What would happen to the arrivals when the server slowed down?

choices.text: Threads make each request faster
choices.why: Each request takes as long as the server makes it; the threads change when requests are sent, not how long they take.

choices.text: urllib refuses a second request on one thread
choices.why: One thread can send as many requests as it likes, one after another.

choices.text: So arrivals keep to the schedule when the server slows
choices.why: Right. A generator that waited for answers would slow down with the server and report a pleasant number.

choices.text: To open one connection and reuse it
choices.why: Each request opens its own connection here.

prompt: In a line of hammer.py's output, what does the done column count?
hint: The notes beside the last part of the program.

choices.text: The answers that arrived during that second
choices.why: Right. That is the throughput the server managed in that second, whichever second the requests were sent in.

choices.text: The requests sent in that second that succeeded
choices.why: sent and errors describe the requests sent in that second; done counts arrivals, from any second.

choices.text: The answers since the run began
choices.why: It is per second, not a running total.

choices.text: The requests the server refused
choices.why: Refusals are counted under errors.

prompt: hammer.py counts a request as an error when it gets a 4xx or 5xx status, when the connection is refused, or when ___ seconds pass with no answer.
In the spike run, seconds 5 to 7 were back at ten requests a second, and the medians were still 923, 439 and 227 ms. Why?
hint: Look at the done column in those seconds.

choices.text: The generator was slowed by its own threads
choices.why: It sent ten a second on schedule; the time was spent waiting for answers.

choices.text: The server was still working off the queue
choices.why: Right. done was 93, 83 and 81 in those seconds: the server was answering requests left over from the spike.

choices.text: Show 990 had sold out during the spike
choices.why: GET requests book nothing; the show page is the same before and after.

choices.text: The database had grown during the spike
choices.why: Nothing was written: every request was a read.

prompt: Put what the stress run showed in the order it happened.
hint: Second 3, second 5, second 7, and after the schedule.

prompt: In the manner of its failure under stress, which describes the box office?
hint: Did anything turn the excess away quickly?

choices.text: It answered the excess with a quick 503
choices.why: Nothing in app.py refuses a request; every one is taken and served in turn.

choices.text: It crashed and stopped answering
choices.why: It kept answering, between 69 and 139 a second, to the end.

choices.text: It served old copies of the page to save time
choices.why: There is no cache in app.py; every request counts the bookings again.

choices.text: Every request queued, and times grew to seconds
choices.why: Right. That is the bad manner: nobody is told to come back later, and everybody waits.

prompt: What would a soak test of the box office watch that hammer.py's output does not show?
hint: Measurements of the server, not of the responses.

choices.text: The median response time of the requests in each second
choices.why: hammer.py prints that already.

choices.text: How many requests the generator sent in each second
choices.why: That is the sent column.

choices.text: Its memory, its open files and the database size
choices.why: Right. What accumulates lives in the server, and lesson 22 collects it.

choices.text: How many errors came back in each second of the run
choices.why: That is the errors column.

prompt: What does taskset -c 0,1 python3 app.py do?

choices.text: Starts two copies of the box office
choices.why: One process; what changes is where it may run.

choices.text: Runs the box office on processors 0 and 1 alone
choices.why: Right. The process may use those two and no others.

choices.text: Gives the box office a scheduling priority of 0 and then 1
choices.why: Priority is nice; taskset sets which processors.

choices.text: Starts it with one thread per processor
choices.why: The threads are the server's own; taskset limits the processors they run on.

prompt: Why was hammer.py started with taskset -c 2,3 in both scalability runs?

choices.text: So it did not compete with the server for processors
choices.why: Right. Kept apart, the server's processors measure the server and not the generator as well.

choices.text: So it would send twice as many requests
choices.why: The schedule sets the rate; the processors do not.

choices.text: Because Python needs two processors to run its threads
choices.why: Python threads run on one processor or several.

choices.text: To make it a second, separate machine
choices.why: It is the same machine, with the work divided between its processors.

prompt: A service carries 50 requests a second at most on one processor and 90 on two. By what factor did its capacity grow? Give a plain number, such as 1.5.
hint: The second capacity divided by the first.

prompt: A booking endpoint carries 25 bookings a second on two processors and 25 on eight. What does that say about it?
hint: What would have to be true for more processors to add nothing?

choices.text: It scales, because nothing failed on either run
choices.why: Scaling is about the ratio between capacities, and 25 to 25 is a ratio of one.

choices.text: The eight-processor run was too short to count
choices.why: A capacity that does not move at all is not a sampling problem.

choices.text: Something in it runs one request at a time
choices.why: Right. A lock held during each booking, like the box office's booking_lock, makes every processor wait in turn.

choices.text: Eight processors are too many for one server
choices.why: More processors do not make a server slower; they just go unused here.

prompt: Which of these results are failures of the test that produced them? Choose every one that is.
hint: Each test has its own meaning of fail.

choices.text: Load test: the 95th percentile is 210 ms against 200 during the hold
choices.why: A fail: the threshold was crossed at the expected load.

choices.text: Stress test: errors begin at 300 requests a second
choices.why: Not a fail: the breaking point is what a stress test is run to find.

choices.text: Spike test: three minutes to normal times, where 30 s was agreed
choices.why: A fail: recovery is half of what a spike test checks, and it took six times too long.

choices.text: Soak test: memory flat across eight hours
choices.why: A pass: the last hour looks like the first.

choices.text: Stress test: one seat sold twice at 400 a second
choices.why: A fail: a wrong result under pressure is a defect whatever the breaking point was.

prompt: A stress staircase finds the show page breaks near 80 requests a second, and the requirement asks for 50. Which test says whether the 10:00 sale of a popular show will be survived?
hint: How does the crowd arrive at 10:00?

choices.text: A soak test at 50 a second
choices.why: A soak asks about drift over hours, and the sale lasts minutes.

choices.text: A longer load test at 50 a second
choices.why: That checks the steady requirement again, which is already met; the sale is not steady.

choices.text: A scalability test on two machines
choices.why: That asks whether resources add capacity, before anybody knows whether more is needed.

choices.text: A spike from normal to the sale's peak
choices.why: Right. A crowd arriving in one minute gives the server no time to adapt, which a slow staircase did.
